**Enhancing Occupancy Models for Black and White Ruffed Lemurs: Integrating Passive Acoustic Monitoring**

**and Vegetation Surveys of Key Tree Species**

Name: Nina Frank

Student ID: 1456415

Supervisor: Fred de Boer

Thesis Code: WEC80436

Date: 07.03.2025

**Abstract**

The black and white ruffed lemur (_Varecia variegata_) is a critically endangered primate, endemic to Madagascar’s eastern rainforests where ongoing anthropogenic changes to the habitat pose severe threats to its survival. Being a highly frugivorous species with a boom-bust reproductive strategy where reproduction is delayed with environmental change, _V. variegata_ is especially sensitive to variables of habitat quality. Still the mechanistic drivers of its distribution and habitat selection remain poorly understood. The species was thought to inhabit primarily pristine forest habitat though it is increasingly found in fragmented and exploited landscapes, contradicting previous assumptions. The particular ecology of the species suggests that the presence of key food and nesting tree species could play a leading role in the occurrence of the species, though this has not been explicitly examined. This study aims to do so and identify the vegetation and landscape variables which influence _V. variegata_ occupancy in Ranomafana National Park in southeastern Madagascar. 20 autonomous acoustic recorders (Audiomoths) will be deployed across 4 sites representing a gradient of habitat disturbance. A convolutional neural network (CNN) will be used to detect the calls and thereby generate presence/absence data of the species. Vegetation surveys within a 400m radius of each Audiomoth will quantify food tree density, canopy cover and resource availability (fruit, leaves, flowers), focusing on ecologically important and dominant plant species. Occurrence data generated with passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) will be analyzed using a Bayesian spatial occupancy model to assess the relationship between distributions of the species and the environmental variables tested while accounting for imperfect detection. The findings will contribute to a better understanding of the habitat requirements of the species and may inform future conservation strategies.

# Introduction

The Black and White Ruffed Lemur (Varecia variegata) is a critically endangered keystone species endemic to the eastern rainforests of Madagascar (Louis et al., 2020). The highly frugivorous black-and-white ruffed lemur plays a crucial role in pollination and seed dispersal within its ecosystem (Moses & Semple, 2011). The main threats to the persistence of the species include habitat degradation and loss due to mining, logging, and slash-and-burn agriculture, with populations estimates suggesting an 80% decline over the past two decades (Louis et al., 2020). These estimates are however based on species densities and occurrences recorded in a few select areas while **exact distributions remain mostly unknown** across its range (Louis et al., 2020). The delineation of the species boundaries and distribution, along with their taxonomic status are of primary concern for their conservation, according to the latest IUCN red list assessment (Louis et al., 2020).

Recent research on the species' distribution has made significant progress in addressing the mentioned knowledge gaps. However, variations in findings suggest that there are still opportunities for further research and improvement. Batist et al. (to be published) used Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) to detect the presence of black and white ruffed lemurs in the COVAF corridor in Madagascar and consequently used occupancy modeling to deduce important habitat factors. They found that NDVI and elevation were the strongest predictors of lemur presence. NDVI was positively associated, and elevation negatively associated with distributions (Batist et al., to be published). The results on elevation do not reflect expected findings, that there is an ideal elevation range from low to mid-altitude forests (up to 1350m) which was previously found (Louis et al., 2020). The findings of Batist et al.’s (to be published) may be influenced by site specific land use patterns, such as increased agricultural land use in the low altitude areas or could be driven by unidentified factors. Another study by Mancini et al. (2023) employed a landscape genetics approach to assess drivers of dispersal. In contrast to Batist et al.’s findings they found NDVI to be negatively associated with dispersion. These unexpected findings may stem from differences in study methods, sites, study area sizes. They could also arise from missing mechanistic determinants of distribution as well as the difficulties of collecting sufficient occurrence data in this difficult habitat.

Due to the particular ecology of _V. variegata_ it may be pivotal to investigate the impact of specific tree species on the species distribution. Fruit constitutes between 70 and 90% of the species’ diet (Beeby & Baden, 2021; Ratsimbazafy, 2006; White et al., 1995). Although preferred food trees vary between seasons, populations and generations, black-and-white ruffed lemurs exhibit a high degree of dietary specialization. Beeby & Baden (2021) found that just five plant species accounted for almost 50% of their diet. While the exact preferred species can differ greatly over time and site, this demonstrates a strong reliance on specific fruiting trees. V. variegata also display reproductive strategies and infant-rearing behaviours which are unique among primates and result in a dependence on certain tree species. Female lemurs build nests to raise and “park” their young while they forage (Baden, 2019). The selection of nesting trees is a specialized behaviour and is tied to the density of feeding trees nearby, the size of the trees as well as proximity to other nests or females (Baden, 2019).

A study by Roman (2017) in a different region of Madagascar found that black-and-white ruffed lemurs were more abundant in undisturbed forests than in historically logged areas. The logged sites had a lower density of large fruiting trees, which are often targeted for timber extraction, suggesting that the availability of key food tree species plays an important role in habitat selection. This and other early research on _V. variegata_ indicated that these specialized, large-bodied frugivores are particularly sensitive to habitat degradation, making them unlikely to thrive in secondary or disturbed forests (Louis et al., 2020; White et al., 1995). However, more recent findings by Petersen et al. (2023) reveal surprising flexibility in black-and-white ruffed lemurs. They have been observed selecting habitats across fragmented and exploited landscapes and have additionally been sighted increasingly in areas with a history of significant anthropogenic disturbance near the Centre ValBio (CVB). These observations suggest that previous studies may have overlooked critical mechanistic determinants of habitat selection. The presence or density of food trees is likely a primary factor influencing habitat suitability and may help explain the earlier mentioned conflicting findings regarding the effects of NDVI and elevation on habitat use.

In order to better understand the mechanistic factors driving V. variegata distribution, and thus better protect their habitat, this study will integrate PAM as used in Batist et al. (to be published) with vegetation plots which will quantify the availability of important food species in Ranomafana National Park. PAM, an emerging and transformative method for detecting species in difficult survey environments (e.g. dense tropical rainforests), enables the collection of extensive occurrence data that would be unfeasible through traditional field methods (Batist et al., to be published). Though the Black and White Ruffed Lemur is suitable for it due to easily distinguishable, loud calls, not many studies have used this method to research this particular species (Batist et al., to be published). By incorporating this powerful occurrence data with key vegetation variables, this research aims to refine occupancy models of V. variegata, enhancing our understanding of its habitat selection and contributing to a key IUCN conservation priority for the species. Additionally, understanding the influence of food tree species can contribute to targeted reforestation projects and inform future agroforestry projects which benefit local communities.

Question and Hypotheses

Research Question:

1. What are the key environmental and vegetation factors influencing habitat selection of the black and white ruffed lemur (_V. variegata_) in Ranomafana National Park?

Hypotheses:

**Vegetation variables** (local scale)

1. Higher densities of known important food tree species will be positively correlated with the occurrence of _V. variegata_, possibly explaining some hypothesized associations with variables discussed below_._
2. A higher proportion of trees bearing fruit and young leaves will be positively associated with the presence of the species (especially in the non-fruiting dry season).
3. There will be a positive correlation of the species’ presence with tree density which will level off at after reaching a threshold.
4. Higher canopy cover will be positively associated with the occurrence of the lemur, as the canopy provides pathways for movement.

**Environmental variables** (larger scale)

1. Forest height will be positively correlated with the presence of the lemur.
2. Higher EVI values will be positively correlated with _V. variegata_ presence.
3. Lemur occurrence will decline in areas which are close to anthropogenic land use such as agriculture, mining, infrastructure etc.

# Methods

- 1. Set up acoustic Recorders
  2. Conduct Vegetation Surveys
  3. Use a machine learning model to determine ruffed lemur presence/ absences
  4. Use an occupancy model to derive the relationship between presence and environmental variables

## Study Species

Varecia variegata are a critically endangered lemur species endemic to Madagascar’s eastern rainforests. They can weigh over 4kg, making them one of the largest living lemur species. Their taxonomic status is yet to be conclusively determined but currently three subspecies are accepted: _V. v. editorium_, _V. v. subcincta_ and _V. v. variegata._ Core group sizes commonly range from 2 to 5 individuals but temporary fission-fusion groupings of 16 to 32 individuals may form in response to food availability during fruiting (Baden et al., 2015). A "boom-bust" reproductive pattern has been observed, in which large litters (2-3, rarely up to 5 individuals) are born during certain years, followed by years with little to no reproduction (Baden, 2019; Louis et al., 2020). It has been observed that environmental changes can prolong years with no reproduction. Newborns are underdeveloped and lack the ability to cling to their mothers in the first few weeks and thus need to be carried orally (Baden, 2019). As this is too energy consuming and dangerous to sustain while foraging, female lemurs engage in nest-building and “park” their young in nests near those of other females. This allows for allo-mothering, or shared caregiving and raises infant survival (Baden, 2019). _V. variegata_ have a characteristically short digestion period and consequently their diet is composed almost entirely of fruit from up to 97 tree species (Beeby & Baden, 2021; Ratsimbazafy, 2006; White et al., 1995). In the non-fruiting season this can be supplemented to varying degrees by young leaves, flowers and even fungi in some regions (Beeby & Baden, 2021; Ratsimbazafy, 2006; White et al., 1995). Their specialized diet makes them important pollinators and seed dispersers. An individual lemur may disperse over 3000 seeds of up to 40 different tree species per month, making it a keystone species of these rainforests (Moses & Semple, 2011).

## Study Site

The research will be conducted in Ranomafana National Park (RNP) in southeastern Madagascar (21°16'S, 47°20'E). The park was established in 1991 and protects 41 600 hectares of endemic tropical rainforest at elevations between 500 to 1500 meters. The climate is humid and rainy tropical climate with temperatures ranging from 15 to 27°C in the rainy fruiting season (November to April) and 8 to 20°C in the dry season (May to October). Average rainfall ranges from 300mm in January to 45mm in September. The occurrence data will be collected across four different study sites (see Figure 1) within Ranomafana National Park, to reflect different levels of habitat disturbance. Fieldwork will take place from September to October 2025 in the dry season.

Mangevo

Mangevo is an undisturbed primary forest site at 800 to 1100m elevation. It is the site of the long-term Ranomafana Ruffed Lemur Project where this species is monitored and studied extensively in its assumed prime habitat.

Valohoaka

Valohoaka is a site with a history of low-intensity human disturbance. It was selectively logged before RNP was established in 1991. While the site remains relatively similar to pristine forests in terms of diversity and structure, its metrics still fall slightly short of those observed in undisturbed areas (Mancini, 2022).

Talatakely

Talatakely reflects an intermittent level of habitat disturbance as the site was intensively logged between 1986 and 1989. There has been significant regrowth since, though the forest remains shorter in height and lower in density than the pristine site (Mancini, 2022).

Sakaroa

Sakaroa is a site which has faced significant anthropogenic change. Before the establishment of RNP, the land was used for agriculture (rice paddies) and humans resided very close. This site reflects extreme changes to the habitat of the black and white ruffed lemur and shows relatively high homogeneity in terms of species diversity and composition (Mancini, 2022).

## Deployment of Audiomoths

_Figure 1 A map displaying the study sites in which the Audiomoths will be displayed (red triangles), adapted from Mancini (2022)_

20 Audiomoths will be deployed in a grid system across these four sites (5 per site). They will use Energizer Ultimate Lithium AA batteries and SanDisk ExtremePro SD cards. Following Batist et al. (to be published) they will record daily between 5am and 8pm (15h per day), as the focal species is diurnal and unlikely to vocalize in the hours outside of these. The Audiomoths have a sample rate of 48kHz, a gain of 30dB and record in a 16-bit mono format.

Roar-shrieks (a common vocalization) can be detected by Audiomoths up to and possibly beyond 400m (Batist et al., 2024) so they will be placed at least 1km apart to avoid pseudo replication. Additionally, close proximity to paths and rivers will be avoided as these may interfere with call identification.

## Vegetation Surveys

**_Figure 2_** _a) A visualization of the method which will be used to gain an overview of the vegetation structure and composition surrounding each Audiomoth. Each cardinal direction will be surveyed four times in 100m intervals, resulting in a 400m radius. b) A visualization of the Point-Centered Quarter Method, from Mitchell (2010)_

Vegetation surveys will be conducted in a 400m radius around each Audiomoth to quantify the density of food trees, the presence of fruit, young leaves, and flowers, the total tree density, canopy cover and DBH within the audio detection range. For each cardinal direction from the center of the plot, four perpendicular transects of 100m with 3-4 survey points each will be conducted at 100-meter intervals, resulting in a total of 48-64 trees per cardinal direction and 192-256 trees per Audiomoth location (Figure 2). A species effort curve will be used during initial surveys to identify the minimum number of trees that must be sampled around each AudioMoth site until food tree density levels off. At each survey point, the Point-Centered Quarter Method (PCQM) will be employed to record trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) larger than 15 cm, consistent with previous findings on food tree selection frequencies (White et al., 1995). This plotless method enhances survey efficiency while maintaining consistency and minimizing subjective bias compared to other methods (Mitchell, 2010).

Given the highly variable and unpredictable diet of _V. variegata_ across different sites, seasons, and groups, it is challenging to extensively survey all potential food sources. However, as these lemurs have been found to derive over 50% of their nutrition from just five species at any given site, as well as feeding on a lower diversity of plant species in the dry season (Beeby & Baden, 2021), it can be inferred that their primary food tree species must be relatively widespread to influence habitat selection in this period. Therefore, the vegetation surveys will be streamlined by focusing on quantifying the presence of food tree species for _V. variegata_ that are among the most ecologically important species identified for each site through extensive vegetation transects conducted by Mancini (2022) between 2015 and 2017. These top species were determined based on relative frequencies (RF), relative densities (RD), and relative dominances (RDo), culminating in the calculation of the Importance Value Index (IVI) (Appendix Table I - IV). Additionally, other known important food tree species will be included in the surveys to minimize chances of missing potentially crucial information. Trees not listed as either known important food trees or ecologically dominant will be noted as unidentified species for the purpose of this study. Additional variables which will be recorded include circumference at 130cm height C<sub>130</sub> to calculate the diameter at breast height DBH; distance to the center, to later calculate tree density in accordance with Mitchell (2010), as well as the presence of fruit, young leaves, and flowers on all surveyed trees. Tree density will be calculated as follows:

1. The mean distance to the center (mdc) will be determined by summing the distances from the eight nearest trees to the center and dividing by eight.
2. Density (trees/m²) will be calculated as 1/mdc.

At the center of each plot, canopy cover will be recorded to provide additional habitat characteristics. This will be estimated by using a toilet paper roll with a transparent dot grid taped over one end. At the center of each plot, the dots which fall over vegetation versus the sky will be counted while looking through the tube.

For each Audiomoth site this data will be averaged to obtain an understanding of the immediately surrounding vegetation and result in the ´vegetation variables listed in Table 1.

# Data Analysis

## CNN

The study will use a convolutional neural network (CNN) pipeline developed by Batist et al. (to be published) with Keras in TensorFlow to identify the call and thus presence of _V. variegata_. It is based on MobileNetV2, pretrained on ImageNet, and modified to classify Black and White Ruffed Lemur calls. The model was trained for 15 epochs with a learning rate of 1×10⁻⁵, with early stopping after five consecutive epochs without improvement. Predictions are made for every 2-second time window. Model performance was evaluated based on false positive rate, recall (prioritized over precision), accuracy, and AUC.

To validate the presence of the lemur in this study, the top 10 daily predictions per site will be manually checked in Arbimons validation interface. The model will be tested with new data and retrained if needed, though it is expected to perform well.

## Occupancy Model

Occupancy modeling will be used to estimate the probability of _V. variegata_ presence while accounting for imperfect detection. Detection/non-detection data will be structured as a matrix, where each row represents a unique recording site (AudioMoth location), and each column represents a sampling day. A value of 1 indicates detection of species calls, and 0 indicates non-detection. Since occupancy models explicitly distinguish between true species presence and detection probability, repeated, daily sampling at the same sites is used to estimate detection probability (rather than treating each detection event as an independent occurrence).

The variables elevation, forest height, forest cover loss, NDVI, EVI and land use & cover (Table 1) will be averaged within the 400m radius buffer zone surrounding each Audiomoth location using the Zonal Statistics tool in QGIS (v3.42) in order to incorporate them in the model.

A Bayesian spatial occupancy model will then be implemented using the spOccupancy R package (Doser & Finley, 2015), incorporating spatial autocorrelation through Gaussian processes. To identify the best-performing model, a sequential modeling approach will be applied:

1. Detection probability models will be evaluated first while holding occupancy probability constant.
2. The best detection model will then be used to assess models for occupancy probability.

Given the limited number of recording sites, the number of environmental variables (Table 1) will be reduced by univariate screening. All covariates will be standardized (to zero-mean and unit-variance) to ensure comparability. Occupancy models will first be run with each covariate separately to assess their individual impact on the model. Covariates with a weak or no relationship with occupancy will be removed, as will those with little variation across sites. Additionally, I will check for collinearity using the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) and remove correlated variables. Final model selection will then be based on Watanabe–Akaike Information Criterion (wAIC) values, with a comparison between spatial and non-spatial models to assess the impact of spatial dependence.

Model fit will be assessed using posterior predictive checks and Bayesian credible intervals.

| **Covariate** | **Source** | **Resolution & Year** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elevation | Terra Advanced Spaceborne Thermal Emission and Reflection (ASTER) Radiometer’s Global Digital Elevation Model (Version 3) | 30m, height in meters, mean pixel value within 400m radius |
| Forest height | Global Land Analysis and Discover (GLAD) team at the University of Maryland, Global Forest Canopy Height (Potapov et al. 2020) | 30m, 2019, height in meters, mean pixel value within 400m radius |
| Forest cover loss | GLAD, developed from a time series analysis of Landsat images (Potapov, 2021) | 30m, 2023, change in pixel from a forest to non-forest state with 0 = no loss, 1:23 = year of change, mean pixel value within 400m radius |
| EVI | to be calculated from surface reflectance data by GLAD ARD (Potapov, 2020) using the formula: EVI = 2.5 \* ((NIR - Red) / (NIR + 6 \* Red - 7.5 \* Blue + 1)) (NIR is the near-infrared band) | 28m, 2024, mean pixel value within 400m radius |
| Global land cover and land use | GLAD, developed from Landsat satellite imagery (Hansen, 2022) | 30m, 2019, mean pixel value within 400m radius |
| Tree density | From own vegetation surveys | 2025 |
| Density of food trees | From own vegetation surveys | 2025 |
| Percentage of trees with fruit/ young leaves/ flowers | From own vegetation surveys | 2025 |
| DBH | From own vegetation surveys | 2025 |
| Canopy cover | From own vegetation surveys | 2025 |
| Habitat disturbance | Pristine, history of selective logging, history of intensive logging, history of agriculture.<br><br>This may be replaced or supplemented with a calculation of a fragmentation index per site (<https://www.fragstats.org/index.php/documentation>) |     |
| NDVI | to be calculated from surface reflectance data by GLAD ARD (Potapov, 2020) using the formula: NDVI = (NIR-R)/(NIR+R) (NIR is the near-infrared band, R is the red band) | 28m, 2024, mean pixel value within 400m radius |

# Working Plan and Time Schedule

Overview of Research Phases

This study will be conducted in the following phases: preparation, data collection, data processing, statistical analysis, and thesis writing. The timeline for each phase is outlined below.

Research Phases and Timeline

Phase 1: Preparation and Planning (February – April 2025)

- Finalize thesis proposal and research methodology.
- Obtain MICET permits for fieldwork..
- Test AudioMoth devices (battery & storage).
- Establish recording locations.
- Prepare for travels (vaccinations, university administration, CVB administration)
- Prepare for data collection (create datasheets, make identification booklet for plant species, print and laminate canopy cover reference, order write in rain notebooks, run through CNN scripts, download, and store environmental layers (NDVI, elevation…)

Phase 2: Data Collection (September – October 2025)

- Deploy 20 AudioMoth devices across three sites with varying disturbance levels.
- Collect acoustic data over 2 months.
- Conduct field surveys to record vegetation variables.
- Service the Audiomoths every ten days.
- Ensure data backup during collection.

Phase 3: Data Processing and Pre-Analysis (October – November 2025)

- Convert and preprocess acoustic recordings.
- Apply the convolutional neural network (CNN) pipeline to detect ruffed lemur calls.
- Structure detection/non-detection data for occupancy modeling.
- Check and clean environmental data for analysis.

Phase 4: Statistical Analysis and Modeling (November – December 2025)

- Conduct exploratory analysis and check for collinearity among variables.
- Fit Bayesian spatial occupancy models using spOccupancy R package.
- Compare non-spatial vs. spatial models using wAIC.
- Validate model performance (posterior predictive checks, manual validation of top CNN predictions).

Phase 5: Interpretation and Thesis Writing (December – February 2025)

- Write an Introduction (problem statement, aim of the research…)
- Interpret the results & discuss limitations.
- Discuss implications for Conservation.
- Make figures, tables, and supplementary materials.

Phase 6: Finalization and Defense (February)

- Revise the draft of thesis.
- Prepare presentation for thesis defense.
- Finalize and submit the thesis.

Preliminary Fieldwork Schedule:

The audio moths need to be serviced every 10-14 days (new batteries and SD cards), meaning the sites need to be visited at regular intervals. Two of the sites (Mangevo and Valohoaka) require overnight expeditions as they are at remote locations in the rainforest. The third site Talatakely and Sakaroa are reachable in a daytrip from the research center. As Mangevo has an active, long term research project going on, there will be people available to service the Audiomoths, and it will require only two trips to deploy and collect Audiomoths, as well as to conduct the vegetation surveys. The days in which no fieldwork is scheduled serve as a buffer (in case expeditions take longer than expected), as well as scheduled time to identify plant material and time to digitally enter, upload and backup data. # Backup Plan

If the data collection or fieldwork does not go to plan and insufficient data for this analysis can be generated, an alternative plan has been established.

Dr. Carly Batist, a researcher who has conducted extensive acoustic studies on the black and white ruffed lemur in the COVAF corridor south of RNP has offered to make her datasets available for analysis. While aspects of this data have been examined a few questions remain unexplored. Two topics could thus serve as alternative research questions:

1. Cyclone impact on the distribution of _V. variegata_: The data collected contains information about the distribution of the species before and after a destructive cyclone. There have been observations of differential habitat use following an extreme weather event such as this (a movement towards crop fields), though a formal analysis of this behaviour has not been conducted (Batist et al., to be published). As cyclones are an important feature in Madagascar’s eastern climate this is an essential pattern to understand and formally analyze.
2. Absence of the species north of RNP: Although there is seemingly suitable habitat for this lemur just north of RNP, the species has not been sighted there, and is only very occasionally heard. The reasons for this have not been determined and would provide an interesting basis for the analysis of acoustic data.

These two projects would provide alternative means to study habitat selection of the species and contribute to its protection in the future.

# Data Storage and Sharing Plan

Primary Data Storage

Audio data from the AudioMoth recorders will be saved onto SanDisk ExtremePro SD cards while they are deployed in the field. Vegetation data will be recorded in a “Rite in the Rain” Notebook (hard copy) and later transferred to an Excel datasheet.

Data Backup Strategy

Data from SD cards will be transferred to an external SSD to prevent loss due to equipment failure or environmental conditions. At the research center where there is an internet connection, data will be uploaded to a cloud platform. The sheet with Vegetation data will also be backed up to an online cloud platform.

Data Organization and Metadata

Files will follow a standardized naming convention (e.g., date, location, recording unit ID, PlotID). Metadata will include details on site conditions, recording settings, and observational context to ensure data usability.

Open Access and Data Sharing

When the project is complete, all cleaned datasets, metadata and relevant scripts will be deposited in an open-access repository to allow further research to use the collected data.
